# Requirements and System Concept {#sec-requirements}

Before any line of code could be written, one question had to be answered. What exactly must the new node do, and what is outside the work of this thesis? This chapter answers it in four steps. It first names where the requirements come from (@sec-req-sources) and collects them in one table (@sec-req-list). It then works out the most important ones with numbers, such as the clock that the PWM needs and the data rate that 25 segments need (@sec-req-analysis). These numbers lead to the design decisions in @sec-req-decisions. The chapter closes with the system architecture that follows from them (@sec-system-architecture).

## Sources of the Requirements {#sec-req-sources}

The requirements come from three AES documents and from meetings with the AES team. The first document is a concept wish list for a planned LED driver IC. It sorts the features into three levels. *Bronze* is the baseline, *Silver* is optional and *Gold* is advanced [@aes_wishlist]. The second document describes the digital part of the concept and the present solution with a microcontroller in every light segment [@aes_digital_requirements]. The third document is the Flexlink specification. It defines the serial protocol between the master and the segments, with its frame format and its commands [@aes_flexlink].

The Bronze level is the mandatory baseline of this thesis. Silver and Gold were not targets. Still, some of their requirements concern the digital part, and the node meets a few of them anyway. Its PWM runs above 600 Hz, for example, and its answers travel back through the chain to the master. These requirements are therefore listed as well, and the column *Level* in @tbl-requirements shows where each one comes from.

Two points help to read the requirements correctly. The wish list describes the whole system. This means the IC or FPGA together with the driver stage, the LEDs and the power supply. A digital design alone cannot meet all of it, so this chapter states for each requirement whether it lies inside the scope of the thesis. The analog parts of the concept, such as the DC-DC converter and the current setting per channel, were moved into a separate "black box" that is not part of this work.

## Requirement List {#sec-req-list}

@tbl-requirements collects all requirements. Each one has an ID from R1 to R21, so the later chapters can refer to it. The column *Level* gives the level in the wish list (B for Bronze, S for Silver, G for Gold). A dash marks a requirement from one of the other AES documents. The column *Type* says whether a requirement describes a function (F), a performance value (P), an interface (I) or a design rule (D). The column *Check* shows how it was verified, by a test on the hardware (T), by simulation (S) or by analysis (A).

: Requirements of the system and their scope in this thesis {#tbl-requirements}

Not all requirements are equally strict. R4 and R7 are hard limits. If the PWM is too slow, the light flickers (@sec-pwm-parameters). If the update takes too long, a passenger sees the light change from one end of the cabin to the other. R2 is fixed as well, because the master sends 16-bit values. Others, such as low power in R14, are goals rather than limits.

A few requirements need a word of explanation. R5 asks that a setting stays until it is changed, so it does not have to be sent again after every power-up. The node keeps its brightness values between two packets. After power-off they are lost, because they live in flip-flops and the FPGA loads its configuration into SRAM. R5 is therefore only met in part. R10 leaves the interface open and only asks for control by an external microcontroller, which this thesis does with Flexlink (@sec-dec-protocol). R11, R13, R16 and R20 belong to the analog part of the concept and lie outside the scope. R12 asks for 3 V to 5 V on the data lines, but the evaluation board only gives about 2.5 V, as @sec-req-io explains.

The Silver and Gold requirements were checked where the design meets them. The measured PWM frequency of 763 Hz lies above the 400 Hz of Bronze (R4) and the 600 Hz of Silver (R17). The 1 kHz of Gold (R19) was not a target and was not tested. The calculation in @sec-req-pwm-clock shows that it would need a clock of at least 65.5 MHz. They carry the ID and a temperature value as Flexlink defines them, not the LED current status or the current setting. The differential data signal of R21 would replace the whole data concept of the Bronze level, so it was not used.

## Requirement Analysis {#sec-req-analysis}

### Clock Frequency for the PWM {#sec-req-pwm-clock}

The PWM generator uses a counter that runs from 0 to $2^N - 1$ and then starts again (@sec-pwm-parameters). One period therefore takes $2^N$ clock cycles, and the PWM frequency is

$$
f_\text{PWM} = \frac{f_\text{clk}}{2^N}
$$ {#eq-req-fpwm}

R2 fixes the resolution at $N = 16$, and R4 asks for more than 400 Hz. Together they set a lower limit for the clock.

$$
f_\text{clk} > 400\ \text{Hz} \cdot 2^{16} = 400\ \text{Hz} \cdot 65{,}536 \approx 26.2\ \text{MHz}
$$ {#eq-req-fclk-min}

The evaluation board has a 10 MHz oscillator (@sec-gatemate). Used directly, this clock would give a PWM frequency of only $10\ \text{MHz} / 65{,}536 \approx 152.6\ \text{Hz}$, which is far below the 400 Hz of the Bronze level. The PLL inside the GateMate was therefore used to raise the clock, and 50 MHz was chosen. This value lies well above the lower limit of 26.2 MHz and is still easy for the design to reach. With this clock the PWM frequency is    

$$
f_\text{PWM} = \frac{50\ \text{MHz}}{65{,}536} \approx 762.9\ \text{Hz}
$$

This is almost twice the Bronze limit, and it also meets Silver with its 600 Hz (R17). Gold asks for more than 1 kHz (R19), which would need at least $1\ \text{kHz} \cdot 65{,}536 \approx 65.5\ \text{MHz}$. The choice of 50 MHz brings two more benefits. At 1 MBaud it gives exactly 50 clock cycles per UART bit, so the bit timing has no rounding error. It also leaves a safe timing margin in the FPGA (@sec-hw-results). The lowest brightness step is one clock cycle of $1 / 50\ \text{MHz} = 20\ \text{ns}$, which is about 0.0015 % of the period.

### Communication Timing for 25 Segments {#sec-req-timing}

R7 asks that the 25th segment has its new data within 25 ms after the first segment starts to receive. Three things decide whether this works. These are the length of the packet, the data rate and the delay inside each node.

Each RGBW segment needs four 16-bit values, which are 8 bytes. An LED packet for $N$ segments therefore holds one SOP, $8N$ data words and one EOP.

$$
N_\text{words} = 8N + 2
$$

For 25 segments this gives 202 words. Each 9-bit word travels as an 11-bit UART frame with one start bit and one stop bit, so one word takes $T_\text{word} = 11 \cdot T_\text{bit}$.

The delay per node depends on how a node forwards the data (@sec-daisy-latency). With store-and-forward, a node first receives the whole rest of the packet and only then sends it on. With cut-through, it passes each word on as soon as the word has arrived, which costs about 10.5 bit times. In a cut-through chain, the last of $N$ nodes has its data once the packet has been sent and each of the $N - 1$ nodes in front of it has added its small delay.

$$
t_\text{CT} = \left[ (8N + 2) \cdot 11 + (N - 1) \cdot 10.5 \right] \cdot T_\text{bit}
$$ {#eq-req-t-ct}

With store-and-forward, every node waits for the whole rest of the packet. Node $k$, counted from the end of the chain, receives $8k + 2$ words, and the waiting times add up.

$$
t_\text{SF} = \sum_{k=1}^{N} (8k + 2) \cdot 11 \cdot T_\text{bit}
$$ {#eq-req-t-sf}

@tbl-req-timing shows the results for 25 segments.

| **Data rate**   | **$T_\text{bit}$** | **Cut-through**  | **Store-and-forward** |
|:----------------|-------------------:|-----------------:|----------------------:|
| 115.2 kBaud     | 8.68 µs            | 21.5 ms          | 253 ms                |
| 250 kBaud       | 4 µs               | 9.9 ms           | 117 ms                |
| 500 kBaud       | 2 µs               | 4.9 ms           | 58.3 ms               |
| **1 MBaud**     | **1 µs**           | **2.47 ms**      | **29.2 ms**           |

: Time until the 25th segment has its data, from @eq-req-t-ct and @eq-req-t-sf {#tbl-req-timing}

The result is clear. Store-and-forward misses the limit even at 1 MBaud, with 29.2 ms against 25 ms. Cut-through at 1 MBaud needs only about 2.47 ms, which is one tenth of the limit. Cut-through would even pass at 115.2 kBaud, but with only 3.5 ms to spare. At 1 MBaud, which is also the rate of the Flexlink specification, the large margin leaves room for the answers on the downlink, for longer packets in later versions and for short gaps between packets.

### I/O Count {#sec-req-io}

Each node needs four serial pins, two for the uplink (`up_rx`, `up_tx`) and two for the downlink (`dn_rx`, `dn_tx`). The node built here drives one RGBW segment and so needs four PWM outputs. With the clock input and the on-board LEDs for testing, the design uses 18 of the 162 I/O pins of the CCGM1A1 (@sec-hw-results). The full AES concept with four RGBW segments per node would need 16 PWM outputs, which would still fit easily.

The voltage level is the real limit. The Pmod connectors of the board pass the signals through a bus switch, and the outputs reach only about 2.5 V (@sec-gatemate). This is below the 3 V to 5 V of R12. For the prototype this was acceptable. The USB-TTL adapter read the 2.5 V signals correctly in every test, and the two GateMates are connected directly to each other. A real system would need a level shifter between the FPGA and the 3 V to 5 V data line, which belongs to the black box from @sec-req-sources.

### Driver Stage {#sec-req-driver}

The low output voltage also shapes the driver stage (R3). Blue and white LEDs need about 3 V or more, so 2.5 V cannot drive them directly. The prototype therefore uses one BS170 N-channel MOSFET per channel as a low-side switch (@sec-low-side-switching), with the LEDs supplied from an external 12 V source. A MOSFET needs no steady gate current, so the FPGA only has to charge a small gate capacitance at each edge [@onsemi_bs170]. This made it a better fit for the weak FPGA output than a bipolar transistor, which needs a base current for as long as it is on.

The price of this choice is the gate voltage. The BS170 is fully specified only at 10 V on the gate, and its threshold can lie anywhere between 0.8 V and 3.0 V [@onsemi_bs170]. At about 2.5 V a typical part switches on, but the datasheet does not promise it for every part. For the prototype, this simple stage was used. Its only task was to make the PWM signals visible on real LEDs during the tests. In the AES system, the LED drivers of the present segments take this role, and they are not part of this thesis. The circuit and its values follow in @sec-hw-driver.

## Design Alternatives and Decisions {#sec-req-decisions}

With the requirements and numbers in hand, several choices had to be made before the design could start. Each of them is explained below, and @tbl-decisions sums them up at the end.

### One FPGA per Segment or One for the Whole Cabin {#sec-dec-topology}

A single central FPGA could drive all segments of the cabin with separate wires. This would need few chips, but every new segment would add more wires, more weight and more points of failure. A small FPGA in every segment, connected in a chain, avoids this. Each node only connects to its two neighbours, so the wiring hardly grows when segments are added (@sec-topologies). This is also how AES builds its chain today (R6). One FPGA per segment, connected in a chain, was therefore chosen.

### Microcontroller or FPGA in Each Segment {#sec-dec-driver-ic}

Today every AES segment has an STM32C011F6 microcontroller [@st_stm32c011]. It receives the Flexlink packet, passes it on, sends the answers back and generates the four PWM signals. Each PWM signal then switches an LED driver that sets the current of its channel. This driver is either a BCR421UFD regulator or a transistor circuit with the BC846AQB-Q [@diodes_bcr421; @nexperia_bc846].

### Master for the Prototype {#sec-dec-master}

In the AES system the master is a PIC microcontroller. The first plan was to test the node with this master. The level shifter that AES provided for the connection did not work as expected, so a PC with a USB-TTL adapter took over the role of the master. This turned out to suit the testing well. A Python program is quick to change, new packets and broken packets can be tried in seconds, and the answers appear on the screen at once. The one difficulty is the ninth data bit, which a normal PC serial port cannot send. It is made with the parity bit (@sec-hw-pc-program). The price is that the time between words is less exact than with a microcontroller. The node does not depend on this time, so the test results are not affected.

### Porting the AES Code or a New Design {#sec-dec-own-design}

AES provided the code of its present PIC-to-segment solution. It was studied carefully. It is written for a processor that works through one task after the other, and it was too complex to carry over to parallel hardware. A new and simpler design was therefore written for the GateMate. It follows the Flexlink format exactly but has its own internal structure, which @sec-rtl describes.

### Asynchronous UART or Synchronous Serial Interface {#sec-dec-protocol}

The wish list leaves the interface open (R10). A synchronous interface such as SPI would need an extra clock line next to every data line. Flexlink instead uses an asynchronous UART with one data line per direction and no clock line [@aes_flexlink; @adi_uart2020]. This means fewer wires along the cabin. It also means that a Flexlink node can work with the existing AES master without any change on the master side. The UART-based Flexlink protocol was therefore used, as agreed with AES, and it fulfils R10 as a custom protocol. The differential signal of the Gold level (R21) was not used, because it would need a different physical layer, while the Flexlink lines are single-ended.

| **Decision**          | **Options**                                   | **Chosen**                    | **Main reason**                                          |
|:----------------------|:----------------------------------------------|:------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------|
| Topology              | one central FPGA / one FPGA per segment       | one FPGA per segment, chained | wiring stays almost constant (R6)                        |
| Segment controller    | microcontroller / FPGA                        | FPGA                          | fixed delay in hardware, RTL reusable for an ASIC (R15)  |
| Master for tests      | PIC microcontroller / PC with adapter         | PC with USB-TTL adapter       | AES level shifter not usable, quick to change            |
| Code base             | port the AES PIC code / new design            | new, simpler design           | PIC code too complex for parallel hardware               |
| Forwarding            | store-and-forward / cut-through               | cut-through                   | only cut-through meets 25 ms (R7)                        |
| Serial interface      | synchronous serial / UART (Flexlink)          | UART (Flexlink)               | fewer wires, works with the AES master                   |
| Driver stage          | bipolar transistor / N-channel MOSFET         | BS170 (MOSFET)                | no steady gate current, small gate capacitance           |
| System clock          | 10 MHz / 50 MHz from the PLL                  | 50 MHz                        | 763 Hz PWM and 50 cycles per bit (R4)                    |

: Summary of the design decisions {#tbl-decisions}

## System Architecture {#sec-system-architecture}

These decisions lead to the architecture in @fig-system-architecture (@sec-introduction). A master sends Flexlink packets on the *uplink* to the first node. Each node keeps its own data and passes the rest on to the next one. On the *downlink*, each node sends its own answer towards the master and then passes on the answers of the nodes behind it. In the prototype the master is a PC, and the chain has two nodes, GM1 and GM2. Both run the same bitstream, and each drives one RGBW segment.

Inside each node the design has four jobs. It receives the uplink words with a UART receiver. It forwards every word that is not meant for it, with as little delay as possible. It stores its own brightness values and turns them into four PWM signals. Finally, it answers on the downlink with its ID and temperature and passes on the answers of the nodes behind it. @sec-rtl shows how these jobs are split into modules. Before that, the data path from the serial input to the PWM output was checked with a model in MATLAB/Simulink, which the next chapter describes.
